demographics: Affects males and females about equally
Most often diagnosed in the second to fourth decade of life
Diagnosis is often delayed for years after symptoms begin

risk_factors.text: Family history of primary antibody deficiency or selective IgA deficiency
Personal or family history of autoimmune disease

family_history: Primary antibody deficiency in a relative
Selective IgA deficiency in a relative

chief_complaints.text: I keep getting sinus and chest infections
I've been losing weight without trying

hpi.onset: Gradual, over months to years; symptoms often begin in adolescence or early adulthood
hpi.duration: Recurrent infections over years, often with a long delay before diagnosis
hpi.progression: Infections become more frequent and harder to clear over time; chronic sinus and lung problems develop, and some patients notice enlarged lymph nodes or an enlarged spleen
hpi.location: Upper and lower respiratory tract most often; also ears, sinuses and gastrointestinal tract
hpi.quality: Repeated bacterial infections that respond slowly to antibiotics and come back after treatment
hpi.severity: Moderate to severe; infections may require repeated antibiotic courses and sometimes hospitalization
hpi.timing: Episodic infections with persistent fatigue between episodes
relieving: Antibiotics help each infection but it keeps coming back
pertinent_negatives: Infections only with unusual organisms rather than common bacteria
Recurrent deep abscesses of skin, liver or brain
Opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia
Recent unprotected sexual contact or injection drug use
Long-term corticosteroid or immunosuppressant use before symptoms began
Recurrent infections limited to one site only

argues_against: Recurrent infections only in one lung lobe
Chronic bloody diarrhea with weight loss

negatives: Lymph node swelling that is painless and rapidly growing

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with recurrent ear and sinus infections, poor growth and failure to gain weight, and the diagnosis is often made earlier than in adults.
Older adults may have a milder infection history but more autoimmune disease, chronic lung disease and lymphoproliferative complications at diagnosis.
Patients already on immunosuppressants may have infections with unusual organisms and a less clear pattern of recurrent common bacterial infections.
missing_classic_features: Infections only with common encapsulated bacteria

general.mild: Well-appearing, well-nourished, no distress; may look tired
general.moderate: Chronically ill-appearing, fatigued, may have audible cough or nasal congestion
general.severe: Ill-appearing, tachypneic, using accessory muscles, may be febrile and diaphoretic
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, in respiratory distress, hypoxic, lethargic or confused

labs.caveat: Anemia from autoimmune hemolysis, chronic disease or malabsorption; normal in many patients.
Immune thrombocytopenia is a well-recognized CVID complication.
Relative lymphopenia is common; absolute counts are more informative.
Low total protein reflects hypogammaglobulinemia; a low globulin gap supports the diagnosis.
Low with protein-losing enteropathy or chronic inflammation.
Nonspecific; rises with active infection or granulomatous disease.
Autoimmune thyroid disease is a common CVID comorbidity.
Low with atrophic gastritis or malabsorption.
Iron deficiency from malabsorption or chronic blood loss.
Proteinuria suggests renal involvement or amyloidosis.

imaging.preferred_when: Chronic productive cough, dyspnea or abnormal spirometry

findings.text: Centrilobular nodules or tree-in-bud opacities from small airway infection
Reticular opacities, ground-glass or nodules in a perilymphatic distribution suggesting granulomatous lymphocytic interstitial lung disease

imaging.preferred_when: Acute respiratory symptoms when pneumonia is suspected

findings.text: Lobar or segmental consolidation consistent with pneumonia

imaging.study: CT of the sinuses without contrast

findings.text: Mucosal thickening of the maxillary or ethmoid sinuses
Air-fluid levels or opacification of the sinuses

imaging.study: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss or suspected lymphoma

findings.text: Bowel wall thickening or mesenteric inflammation suggesting inflammatory bowel disease

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected lymphoma or granulomatous disease when CT is equivocal

findings.text: Hypermetabolic lymph nodes or organ involvement
Diffuse splenic or bone marrow uptake

initial.why: Screens for autoimmune cytopenias and assesses overall blood counts
Low total protein and globulin gap suggest hypogammaglobulinemia; assesses liver and kidney function
Baseline inflammatory marker; helps track infection and granulomatous disease
Nonspecific marker of inflammation or underlying lymphoproliferative disease

initial.only_if: pneumonia is suspected (fever, productive cough, hypoxemia or abnormal lung exam)

initial.why: Detects bronchiectasis and interstitial lung disease
initial.only_if: chronic productive cough, dyspnea or abnormal spirometry

initial.test: CT of the sinuses without contrast

confirmatory.why: Shows marked reduction in IgG with low IgA and/or IgM, the hallmark of CVID

confirmatory.test: Specific antibody response to vaccines (tetanus, diphtheria, pneumococcal)
confirmatory.why: Demonstrates impaired functional antibody production after immunization

confirmatory.test: Lymphocyte subset panel (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19, CD16/56)
confirmatory.why: Confirms normal or low B cells with absent plasma cells and helps exclude other immunodeficiencies

supporting.why: Excludes HIV as a cause of recurrent infections and low immunoglobulins
Documents the polyclonal decrease in gammaglobulins and excludes a monoclonal gammopathy

supporting.test: Flow cytometry for B-cell subsets (switched memory B cells)
supporting.why: Low switched memory B cells support the diagnosis and correlate with complications

supporting.test: Stool studies for malabsorption (fecal fat, stool culture, ova and parasites)

supporting.why: Evaluates malabsorption, granulomatous disease or lymphoma
supporting.only_if: chronic diarrhea, weight loss or suspected enteropathy

not_indicated.why: Not routine in the absence of acute respiratory symptoms
not_indicated.only_if: pneumonia is suspected (fever, productive cough, hypoxemia or abnormal lung exam)

not_indicated.why: Not routine without chronic respiratory symptoms or abnormal spirometry
not_indicated.only_if: chronic productive cough, dyspnea or abnormal spirometry

not_indicated.test: CT of the sinuses without contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine without chronic or recurrent sinus symptoms

not_indicated.test: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Not routine without abdominal symptoms or suspected lymphoma
not_indicated.only_if: abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss or suspected lymphoma

not_indicated.why: Not routine; reserved for suspected malignancy or granulomatous disease
No role in the evaluation of immunodeficiency
Not indicated without epigastric pain suggesting pancreatitis
Not indicated without chest pain or cardiac symptoms

decision_points: Do not start immunoglobulin replacement before immunoglobulin levels and vaccine responses are drawn, because treatment will mask the diagnostic findings
Exclude HIV and medication-induced hypogammaglobulinemia (for example rituximab, anticonvulsants) before diagnosing CVID
Check for autoimmune cytopenias and lymphoproliferative disease at diagnosis and during follow-up
Vaccinate with inactivated vaccines; live vaccines are generally contraindicated

criteria.name: CVID diagnosis (ESID/PAGID-style, paraphrased)
criteria.summary: Marked decrease in serum IgG (at least 2 standard deviations below age-matched normal) with low IgA and/or IgM, impaired vaccine antibody responses, onset after 2 years of age, and no other defined cause of hypogammaglobulinemia.
items: Low serum IgG with low IgA and/or IgM
Poor or absent specific antibody response to vaccines

differential.name: HIV infection
differential.why_considered: Recurrent infections, weight loss and fatigue with low immunoglobulins can occur in advanced HIV
differential.trigger: Any adult with recurrent infections and weight loss who has not been tested for HIV

history: Unprotected sexual contact, injection drug use or other exposure risk
Opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis pneumonia, esophageal candidiasis or disseminated mycobacterial disease
Infections with unusual organisms rather than common encapsulated bacteria
labs: Positive HIV antibody/antigen or HIV RNA test
Low CD4 count with an inverted CD4:CD8 ratio
Immunoglobulins are usually normal or elevated, not low

differential.name: X-linked agammaglobulinemia
differential.why_considered: Severe hypogammaglobulinemia with recurrent sinopulmonary infections
differential.trigger: Recurrent infections starting in infancy or early childhood in a boy with absent B cells

history: Symptoms begin in the first 1–2 years of life, after maternal antibodies wane
Male relatives with a similar infection pattern
exam: Absent or very small tonsils and no palpable lymphoid tissue
labs: All immunoglobulin isotypes markedly reduced, including IgM and IgA
Absent or near-absent CD19+ B cells
No B cells on flow cytometry

differential.name: Selective IgA deficiency
differential.why_considered: Recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections with an immunoglobulin abnormality

history: Family history of IgA deficiency or CVID
labs: Serum IgA below the age-matched normal range
Specific antibody responses to vaccines are intact

differential.name: IgG subclass deficiency
differential.why_considered: Recurrent respiratory infections with a subtle antibody defect

history: Recurrent sinusitis, otitis media or bronchitis
Infections often respond well to antibiotics
labs: Total IgG is normal or near normal
One or more IgG subclasses are low
Vaccine antibody responses may be reduced but are often preserved

differential.name: Drug-induced hypogammaglobulinemia
differential.why_considered: Low immunoglobulins and recurrent infections in a patient taking an immunosuppressive medication

history: Current or recent rituximab, anticonvulsant, corticosteroid or other immunosuppressant use
Symptoms began after the medication was started
labs: Low IgG that improves after the offending drug is stopped
B-cell depletion on flow cytometry if rituximab was used

differential.name: Protein-losing enteropathy or nephrotic syndrome
differential.why_considered: Low serum immunoglobulins from loss of protein rather than impaired production

history: Chronic diarrhea, edema or frothy urine
No lifelong pattern of recurrent infections
labs: Low serum albumin and total protein
Elevated stool alpha-1 antitrypsin or heavy proteinuria
Immunoglobulins improve when the protein loss is treated

differential.name: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
differential.why_considered: Older adults with recurrent infections and low immunoglobulins

history: Incidental lymphocytosis on a routine blood count
labs: Marked absolute lymphocytosis with a clonal B-cell population on flow cytometry
Hypogammaglobulinemia may be present but is secondary to the leukemia

severity.mild: Occasional sinopulmonary infections that respond to oral antibiotics; no bronchiectasis or organ damage; normal daily activity
severity.moderate: Frequent or recurrent infections requiring repeated or prolonged antibiotics, chronic sinusitis, early bronchiectasis, fatigue and missed work or school
severity.severe: Infections requiring hospitalization or intravenous antibiotics, established bronchiectasis with chronic sputum and dyspnea, autoimmune cytopenias or significant weight loss
severity.critical: Life-threatening infection such as sepsis, meningitis or severe pneumonia with respiratory failure; or a lymphoproliferative or granulomatous complication causing organ failure

red_flags.finding: Hypotension, tachycardia or altered mental status during an infection
red_flags.meaning: Sepsis; needs immediate resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics
Severe pneumonia or respiratory failure; consider ICU-level care

red_flags.finding: Neck stiffness, severe headache or photophobia
red_flags.meaning: Possible bacterial meningitis; requires urgent lumbar puncture and antibiotics

red_flags.finding: Rapidly enlarging, painless lymph nodes or night sweats
red_flags.meaning: Suspected lymphoma; needs urgent imaging and biopsy

red_flags.finding: New severe anemia, petechiae or bleeding
red_flags.meaning: Autoimmune cytopenia; assess for immune thrombocytopenia or hemolytic anemia

red_flags.finding: Persistent fever with weight loss and no clear source
red_flags.meaning: Occult infection, granulomatous disease or malignancy; broaden the workup

complications.name: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections
clues: Repeated sinusitis, otitis media or pneumonia
Infections that respond slowly to antibiotics and recur after treatment

complications.name: Bronchiectasis
clues: Dilated thick-walled airways on high-resolution chest CT

complications.name: Granulomatous lymphocytic interstitial lung disease
clues: Reticular or nodular opacities on chest imaging
Restrictive pattern on pulmonary function tests

complications.name: Lymphoma
clues: B symptoms such as fever, night sweats and weight loss

complications.name: Gastric cancer
clues: Dyspepsia, early satiety or weight loss
Gastric mass or thickened folds on endoscopy

complications.name: Chronic gastrointestinal disease with malabsorption
clues: Villous atrophy or granulomas on duodenal biopsy

special_populations.differences: May present with recurrent ear and sinus infections, poor growth and failure to gain weight; diagnosis is often made earlier than in adults, and live vaccines are contraindicated.
May have a milder infection history but more autoimmune disease, chronic lung disease and lymphoproliferative complications at diagnosis; higher risk of gastric cancer and lymphoma.
Immunoglobulin replacement should be continued; monitor for infection and autoimmune cytopenias, and coordinate care with immunology and obstetrics.

Patients already on immunosuppressants may have infections with unusual organisms and a less clear pattern of recurrent common bacterial infections; immunoglobulin levels and vaccine responses must be interpreted with caution.

key_questions.question: How many infections have you had in the past year that needed antibiotics, and what kinds were they?
key_questions.looking_for: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections (sinusitis, otitis media, bronchitis, pneumonia) over years, often several per year

key_questions.question: When did these infections start?
key_questions.looking_for: Onset after age 2 years, often in adolescence or early adulthood, with a long delay before diagnosis

key_questions.question: Do the infections clear with antibiotics, and do they come back after treatment?
key_questions.looking_for: Slow response to antibiotics with recurrence after finishing treatment

key_questions.question: Have you ever had pneumonia, and how many times?
key_questions.looking_for: One or more documented pneumonias, sometimes requiring hospitalization

key_questions.question: Have you had chronic sinus or ear problems, or a cough with sputum that never fully goes away?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic rhinosinusitis, recurrent otitis media, chronic productive cough suggesting bronchiectasis

key_questions.question: Have you had diarrhea, weight loss or trouble absorbing food?
key_questions.looking_for: Chronic gastrointestinal disease with malabsorption, a common CVID complication

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swollen lymph nodes, an enlarged spleen, or unexplained fevers and night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Lymphoproliferative or granulomatous complications, including lymphoma

key_questions.question: Have you been diagnosed with an autoimmune condition such as low blood counts, thyroid disease or inflammatory bowel disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Autoimmune cytopenias, autoimmune thyroid disease or IBD, all associated with CVID

key_questions.question: Are you taking any immunosuppressive medications, such as rituximab, corticosteroids or anticonvulsants?
key_questions.looking_for: Drug-induced hypogammaglobulinemia, which must be excluded before diagnosing CVID

key_questions.question: Has anyone in your family had a primary antibody deficiency, selective IgA deficiency or repeated infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of primary antibody deficiency or selective IgA deficiency

key_questions.question: Have you ever had an HIV test, or any risk factors such as unprotected sex or injection drug use?
key_questions.looking_for: HIV infection, which can mimic recurrent infections with low immunoglobulins

key_questions.question: Have you had infections with unusual organisms, deep abscesses, or infections that started in infancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Features suggesting a different immunodeficiency, such as X-linked agammaglobulinemia or an opportunistic infection

reasoning_points: Recurrent sinopulmonary infections over years, often with a long delay before diagnosis
Marked reduction in serum IgG with low IgA and/or IgM
Impaired specific antibody response to vaccines
Onset after age 2 years, with secondary causes of hypogammaglobulinemia excluded
HIV and drug-induced hypogammaglobulinemia ruled out
Associated autoimmune cytopenias, bronchiectasis or lymphoproliferative complications considered
Immunoglobulin replacement should not be started before diagnostic immunoglobulin levels and vaccine responses are drawn

easy: Young adult with years of recurrent sinus and ear infections and several pneumonias
Low total protein with a low globulin gap on routine labs
Markedly low IgG with low IgA and IgM on immunoglobulin panel
Poor vaccine antibody response to tetanus and pneumococcal vaccines
medium: Patient with chronic diarrhea and weight loss in addition to respiratory infections
Autoimmune thrombocytopenia or hemolytic anemia as the presenting problem
Chronic productive cough with bronchiectasis on chest CT
Older adult with recurrent infections and low immunoglobulins who also needs CLL excluded
hard: Patient already on rituximab or another immunosuppressant, making drug-induced hypogammaglobulinemia hard to separate from CVID
Mild or atypical infection history with mainly autoimmune or granulomatous features
Child with recurrent ear and sinus infections and poor growth, where X-linked agammaglobulinemia must be excluded
Patient with low immunoglobulins from protein-losing enteropathy or nephrotic syndrome rather than impaired production
